b: In the early 2010s, two artists, Wura-Natasha Ogunji and ruby onyinyechi amanze, left the US and UK for Nigeria. Unbeknownst to them, they would soon meet and spark a friendship that would birth multiple collaborative works. In Ogunji’s Queens (2013), the artists presented a durational performance, in which they formed several pounds of traditional Yoruba fabric into crowns and sat under the hot sun on Lagos’s Bar Beach. A strip of cloth running from one “crown” to the other connected them to each other like an umbilical cord. Queens exemplifies how amanze and Ogunji artistically express their connection and shared identity as Nigerian women who spent their formative years outside of the country. Their performance critiques the social expectations of women in Nigeria. As author Bimbola Akinbola writes in Transatlantic Disbelonging: Unruliness, Pleasure, and Play in Nigerian Diasporic Women’s Art, “In wearing a crown there is both honor and difficulty due to its weight.”

Such joint performances allow the artists to share this burden and demand witness to their particular subjectivities “in a context of their own creation.” As Akinbola writes of amanze and Ogunji’s work Twin: Art + Performance (2013), in which the artists stand on one side of a length of plexiglass and improvise drawings, “although the performance is happening in New York, [amanze and Ogunji] are also elsewhere, looking out at us through the world they have created.”

The bond between the two artists is a paramount example of “disbelonging,” the expansive and ungovernable attachment that Akinbola’s book conceptualizes. Generative of distinctive visions of diasporic womanhood, the artists’ kinship operates outside of the heteronormative bonds of family and creates a transformative sense of home for both amanze and Ogunji. In these ways, they mirror the pair at the heart of Kenyan filmmaker Wanuri Kahiu’s 2018 queer romance film Rafiki (which in Swahili means “friend”). Through Ogunji and amanze especially, Transatlantic Disbelonging demonstrates how diasporic Nigerian women artists imagine home as rooted in people—in loved ones—rather than a strictly geographic sense of belonging.

In the preface to her book, Akinbola vividly describes Batik Arts, the Missouri store and community created and run by her artist mother and father. Akinbola paints a particularly evocative portrait of her late mother, noting the warm-hearted, wearable art–maker’s propensity for chewing bubblegum. The image of this young immigrant mother popping Dubble Bubble in the gathering place she convened for creatives calls to mind Afrobubblegum: the aesthetic, collective, and brand originated by Kahiu. Afrobubblegum pushes back against the troubling expectation for African cinema to grapple with themes of oppression and struggle alone. Instead, Kahiu argues that African film has the right to be fun and frivolous. The distinct visual language of Rafiki, marked by soft focus shots filled with warm pink and lavender tones, functions as a vehicle for what Kyèra Sterling calls the “transformative self-definition” of the film’s protagonists.1 The two young women construct a new sense of identity by embracing their romantic desire for each other. Kahiu’s themes—queerness, the ongoing need to challenge narrow perceptions of Africa, critical representations of African womanhood across mediums, and the art of making home spaces—directly relate to Akinbola’s project.

Similarly to Afrobubblegum’s boundary-pushing approach to African cinema, Transatlantic Disbelonging broadens the focus in studies of diaspora beyond the losses that migration can entail; and it does so by centering the ways that women artists of Nigerian descent courageously define themselves and create homes within and beyond their country of origin.

Transatlantic Disbelonging highlights how Nigerian women artists push back against normative practices that communities in and outside of the homeland demand of women in exchange for a sense of belonging.

Akinbola’s book arrives at a time when xenophobic hostility legitimized as policy escalates at dizzying speeds. The ability of Nigerians like Akinbola’s parents to immigrate to the United States is currently obstructed. As of January 2026, the US has blocked the entry of Nigerian immigrants, as well as Nigerians on nonimmigrant visas, and paused immigrant visa processes for Nigerians and others. The stated justification for this decision implies that these migrants will be a “financial burden to Americans.”2

Akinbola’s book examines geographic movement from the perspective of Nigerian women migrants and through the creative expression of their experiences. By centering these filmmakers, performers, painters, and writers, Transatlantic Disbelonging affirms the inherent value and richly complex interiority of migrants despite the white nationalist authoritarianism that seeks to portray them as parasites.

A further consequence of Transatlantic Disbelonging is the valuable contribution it makes to African studies, but also crucially to Black studies, which teaches us to study the continent alongside its diaspora. Dwelling on women artists with shared Nigerian roots but different ethnicities, migration stories, and self-identifications, Akinbola offers insights into gendered experiences of Blackness in Nigeria as well as in the United States and United Kingdom. Sharing recent African lineage with those on the continent, yet globally dispersed like members of historic diasporas, diasporic Nigerians occupy a liminal and potent position as Black subjects. Transatlantic Disbelonging carves out fresh space for the consideration of this positionality with a focus on women, who are often marginalized in diasporic narratives.

The book highlights how Nigerian women artists push back against normative practices that communities in and outside of the homeland demand of women in exchange for a sense of belonging. Akinbola explains meticulously how these practitioners perform acts of disbelonging through their inventive and hybrid visual and literary languages, their collaborations, and their self-definitions, which strategically refuse dominant notions of respectability, value, and authenticity. But the book does not speak to Nigeria alone—as Akinbola states, this “‘micro’ study of the African diaspora brings to light [overlooked] negotiations, cultural exchanges, and border crossings … to provide a fuller understanding of black subject formations that are not solely beholden to colonial understandings of place.”

If the cord between identity and nation were loosened, how could we understand what it means to be a Nigerian woman? The Transatlantic artists—Ogunji, amanze, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, Zina Saro-Wiwa, and Nnedi Okorafor—answer in resonant ways.

The role of the ada in Igbo culture provides a specific example of the pressures faced by Nigerian women. As Akinbola explains, the ada, or eldest daughter, is essentially expected to act as a third parent in the Igbo family—as a caretaker of siblings and a leader. This substantial responsibility, borne from childhood, is part of the reason why eldest daughters are respected, but it can also stifle the ada’s ability to prioritize herself.

A neon-yellow figure that amanze calls ada the Alien recurs across the artist’s drawings and offers an example of how Akinbola’s book examines migration through artistic practice. Akinbola illustrates how amanze’s drawings “[offer] another way for the eldest daughter” through this character. In Ogbonno Soup Is Sweeter Since We Met (2014), ada the Alien lies with audre the Leopard, a figure with a leopard head and human arms. Cradled by audre, the ada rests from her duties of pouring into others and herself experiences care. In this work, ada the Alien’s body resembles that of a child, indicating how, in the world that amanze creates, the ada can relinquish her senior status in the family and experience a different position. ada the Alien carves out space to meditate on the childhood of the parentified ada and to imagine possibilities beyond her predetermined role. audre mothers the ada, which calls to mind the maternal relation suggested in the Queens performance.

In one of the book’s most tender moments, Akinbola reveals that for amanze, audre the Leopard is Ogunji. Noting that this caring figure represents amanze’s collaborator illuminates how close friendship between diasporic Nigerian women can enable an alternative sense of belonging. The embrace in amanze’s artwork depicts this disbelonging as deeply restorative.

Akinbola’s book makes a pivotal intervention through its engagement with the taboo—the sexual, the erotic, the queer—in the context of diaspora. This gesture comes alive in the chapter on Njideka Akunyili Crosby, which demonstrates how the visual artist’s paintings use “the erotic to defiantly linger in the space between longing for homeland and the pleasure of making a home elsewhere.” The erotic electrifies a series of depictions of Akunyili Crosby’s relationship with her husband. Taking up the torch from scholars like L. H. Stallings, who have explored similar themes in their research on Blackness, Akinbola’s chapter not only looks boldly at these paintings but also addresses how criticism of Akunyili Crosby’s work has tiptoed around these works. Paintings such as The Bridge (2010) and Re-branding My Love (2011), versions of the same amorous bedroom scene, frame how Akunyili Crosby’s marriage crosses racial and cultural lines.

Akinbola unpacks how they also violate the boundaries of the normative behavior expected of Igbo women, particularly those who belong to the middle class. Nigerian women bear the responsibility of transmitting culture to future generations. Interracial relationships like Akunyili Crosby’s, and furthermore, her erotic renderings of herself, seem to threaten this structure. But through these paintings, the artist creates worlds in which all of her cultural references, memories, and affiliations can coexist. Partially nude or fully undressed, entangled with her husband, and engaged in displays of affection, Akunyili Crosby’s self-representations envision all parts of her at ease in a home of her making.

Akinbola further develops a notion of the erotic as a source of agency in her discussion of filmmaker and installation artist Zina Saro-Wiwa. This chapter argues that in visualizing the erotic agency of the Black body in particular, Saro-Wiwa “acknowledges and resists the burden of respectability … that [hides and dismisses] the importance of emotional expression, intimacy, and vulnerability in the lives of African and African diasporic people.” In Eaten by the Heart: The Documentaries and Eaten by the Heart: The Installation (2012), Saro-Wiwa explores why Africans of diverse nationalities consider kissing in public inappropriate. Akinbola notes how “the shadow of familial expectation and cultural burden [that] African and African diasporic women in particular must consider” can shape these views of affection. By asking her participants “how Africans kiss,” Saro-Wiwa creates a space outside the gaze of the heteronuclear family and of her subject’s respective cultures where they can examine their thoughts and feelings about desire and indeed, make out. Subjects respond by losing themselves in French kissing (a term that further reveals the distancing of the erotic from African cultures), sinking fingers into tight coils, and devouring each other with their eyes.

Through this, Akinbola argues, they reclaim their right to the erotic, asserting that “the violence of colonialism does not strip the ability to love, to feel, to be soft.” Furthermore, the exhibition of these works provides the opportunity for audiences to visually associate romance with Africanness, thereby normalizing the erotic as part of African and diasporic experience.

For Akinbola, “queer” refers to “the gap between the artists … and the myths surrounding nation and womanhood” and diverse ways of thinking about social reproduction. The chapter on novelist Nnedi Okorafor’s 2011 book Akata Witch recognizes queerness in characters who straddle the categories of biological family and chosen family as well as the borders between human and non-human identity. As Akinbola writes, “Okorafor asks us to reconsider how we view and understand normativity, creating an entire world where nonnormative bodies hold power, authority, and unique perspectives.”

In the book’s discourse on disbelonging, queerness is a powerful tool for creatively resisting the constricting conventions with which diasporic Nigerian women wrestle. Though Transatlantic Disbelonging engages generatively with these interpretations of queerness, the book seems to avoid engaging with same-sex desire itself. For example, Saro-Wiwa’s chapter mentions that two women kiss in Eaten by the Heart, but the conversation abruptly truncates there. How could Saro-Wiwa’s inclusion of a queer couple enrich her aim of illustrating Africans’ erotic agency? Given the vital work Akinbola does to confront taboos, the book’s treatment of queerness raises the question of why the presence and possibilities of queer desire are not more deeply considered.

Still, Transatlantic Disbelonging is a carefully crafted and lushly articulated analysis of the critiquing and making of home by a cohort of talented and consequential women artists. The book expands conceptions of Nigeria and Nigerian womanhood through its focus on the unruly artistic practices of the diaspora. Akinbola offers a heightened sense of possibility and even healing to Nigerian women like this author, and to all readers, a space to reflect on questions of autonomy, creativity, and belonging in their own contexts.
